10162-dio-s-rome-volume-3-an-historical-:
Herbert Baldwin Foster translated this third volume of Dio Cassius in 1906, covering Roman history from 44 to 29 BC. Dio, a Greek senator of the third century AD, wrote his long narrative under emperors from Septimius Severus to Alexander Severus. Foster's volume holds the extant books numbered 45 through 51.

Those books follow Octavian, later Augustus, as he rises after Caesar's death, clashes with Antony, and faces Pompey's son Sextus. Cicero's speeches against Antony fill much of the account. Readers get a key ancient source for the fall of the Republic, in clear modern English.
10883-dio-s-rome-volume-4-an-historical-:
Cassius Dio's Roman history, written in Greek under the Severan emperors, continues here in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English translation. This fourth volume covers books 52 through 60, from 29 BC to AD 54, spanning Augustus's settlement of power and the reigns that followed. Each book opens with a summary of its chapters, so readers can find episodes quickly.

Inside, Augustus debates with Agrippa and Maecenas whether to lay down his power, then builds the imperial system instead. Later books follow campaigns, court politics, and the machinery of rule. Dio wrote centuries after some events but close to others, and his narrative remains a central source for how Rome moved from republic to empire.
10890-dio-s-rome-volume-5-an-historical-:
Cassius Dio's Roman History, written in Greek under Septimius Severus and his successors, appears here in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English version. This fifth volume covers extant books sixty-one through seventy-six, from A.D. 54 to 211. It opens with Nero seizing the sovereignty, and runs through emperors, wars, and court intrigue to the early third century.

Dio writes as a senator-historian, close to power and sharp on character. Foster's translation, made while professor of Greek at Lehigh, keeps the narrative clear. Readers get Rome's most turbulent century, from Nero to the Severans, in a primary source of lasting weight.
11278-folk-tales-of-napoleon-napoleonder:
Translated with an introduction by George Kennan in 1902, this volume pairs two folk portraits of Napoleon: Napoleonder from the Russian, and Balzac's Napoleon of the People from the French. The Russian tale opens with God holding a council of angels to punish a wicked world, rejecting earthquake, famine, and flood before settling on a scourge. Peasants call Napoleon Napoleonder, adding a syllable because Napoleon alone sounds clipped to their ears.

Kennan's introduction explains the folk process that turned an emperor into a legend. Balzac's companion piece gives the French popular view. Together the tales show how ordinary people across Europe mythologized the same man in opposite ways, as punishment and as hero.
11607-dio-s-rome-volume-2-an-historical-:
Herbert Baldwin Foster's English version of Dio's Rome, second volume, covers extant books 36 to 44, from 69 to 44 before Christ. Metellus subdues Crete by force, while Mithridates and Tigranes renew the war. Lucullus takes Tigranocerta and Nisibis, then loses the Armenias as his army rises against him.

Later books follow Caesar in Gaul, his garrisons, legal penalties, levies of money, and assignment of tribute. Parties are reconciled, some willingly and others overcome in war, and trouble ends in the consulship of Lucius Paulus and Gaius Marcellus in 50 before Christ. The volume is a Roman history written in Greek under later emperors.
12061-dio-s-rome-volume-6-an-historical-:
Volume 6 of Dio's Rome, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English translation, presents an historical narrative originally composed in Greek. It covers the reigns of Septimius Severus, Geta and Caracalla, Macrinus, Elagabalus, and Alexander Severus. Foster, of Harvard and Johns Hopkins and acting professor of Greek at Lehigh, gives books 77 to 80, covering A.D. 211 to 229, with fragments of books 1 to 21.

Dio Cassius wrote as a senator and historian of an empire in crisis. This volume covers the murderous successions after Septimius Severus, when emperors rose and fell by army and palace intrigue. Foster's translation, with its fragmentary early books, lets English readers follow Rome's third-century turmoil in the words of a contemporary witness.
13552-ceylon-an-account-of-the-island-ph:
Sir James Emerson Tennent gives Ceylon in volume one, fourth edition thoroughly revised in 1860, with maps, plans, and drawings. Physical geography opens with geology, mineralogy, and gems, praising the island's singular beauty, while later parts treat history, topography, natural history, antiquities, and productions.

Voyagers, Tennent notes, wrote of loveliness, brilliant jewels, rich pearls, sagacious elephants, and delicate spices, but said little of inhabitants, showing how little intercourse existed. Lists of birds, from Eulabes religiosa to Passer Indicus, fill natural history pages, and a frontispiece shows noosing wild elephants. The volume is a Victorian survey of an island colony in full detail.
18047-dio-s-rome-volume-1-an-historical-:
Herbert Baldwin Foster turned Dio's Rome into English, first volume, printed in Troy, New York, in 1905 by Pafraets. Dio Cassius wrote his Roman history in Greek under the Severan emperors, and Foster, a professor of Greek at Lehigh, gives it fresh English form.

This volume gathers gleanings from the lost books: the epitome of books one to twenty-one by Zonaras, a monk of Mount Athos about 1130, plus fragments of books twenty-two to thirty-five. The tale runs from Rome's clash with Carthage over Tarentum to the Punic wars. It is a key source for Roman history, in a scholar's careful version.
20360-no-abolition-of-slavery-or-the-uni:
No Abolition of Slavery is a poem against ending the slave trade, cast as satire. In a stall three feet by four, a hump-backed cobbler drinks saloop. With him the muse shall sit and think, the poem declares. He shall complain, in sentimental strain, that negroes are oppressed.

The poem mocks such pity as false feeling in cheap print. Its title calls love's universal empire the true bar to abolition. Modern readers meet here the ugly case made for slavery in verse. The poem stands as evidence of the fight abolition had to win.
20804-lucretia-borgia-according-to-origi:
Old Roman houses still charm the historian in Lucretia Borgia, drawn from source papers. The Colonna, Orsini, and Gaetani families aided the work with open hands. Their aid let the writer test legend against records. Letters and lives could then speak for themselves.

Ferdinand Gregorovius sought the real Lucretia behind centuries of dark tales. Poison myths give way to a woman used by her family's vast plans. Rome, Ferrara, and the Borgia court fill the backdrop. The book counts as a model of history built from documents. It still shapes how readers judge Lucretia today.
24598-a-modern-history-from-the-time-of-:
John Lord wrote this modern history for schools and colleges, from the time of Luther to the fall of Napoleon. It surveys the Reformation, the wars of religion, the rise of modern states, and the French Revolution, ending with Napoleon's downfall. Lord writes for students, not scholars, in clear narrative chapters.

Later pages follow kings, ministers, and peoples through three centuries of change, with notes on culture and ideas beside battles and treaties. The book was a popular American textbook of its age. Readers who want a single-volume survey of early modern Europe will find it readable, opinionated, and full of story.
31907-ancient-pottery-of-the-mississippi:
William H. Holmes's Ancient Pottery of the Mississippi Valley, a Smithsonian Institution Bureau of Ethnology report, surveys the pottery of the middle Mississippi, upper Mississippi, and Gulf provinces. Its contents move from ceramic groups and distribution, age, use, construction, material, color, and form to ornament, modification of shape, and classification of forms.

Later sections describe bowls, pot-shaped vessels, wide-mouthed bottles and jars, and high-necked bottles, each with ordinary, eccentric, and life forms illustrated. Readers get a foundational work of American archaeology, cataloging the vessels of mound-building peoples with careful drawings and description.
3650-selections-from-american-poetry-wit:
Margaret Sprague Carhart edits an anthology of American poetry that runs from colonial times to the nineteenth century. Contents open with Anne Bradstreet's Contemplation and Michael Wigglesworth's Day of Doom, then move through Philip Freneau, Francis Hopkinson's Battle of the Kegs, Joseph Hopkinson's Hail Columbia, and Timothy Dwight. Later sections reach Poe, Longfellow, Lowell, and Whittier.

Carhart adds an introduction to guide students through the growth of American verse. The selections show how poetry moved from Puritan meditation and patriotic song to romantic lyric and narrative. The book suits students and general readers who want a single, chronological shelf of American poems.
5790-aria-da-capo:
Millay's Aria da Capo is a one-act play from 1920, set on a stage dressed for a harlequinade in merry black and white. Its persons are Pierrot, Columbine, Cothurnus as the mask of tragedy, and two shepherds, Thyrsis and Corydon. The curtain rises behind the footlights on a world that is at once a comedy stage and a field where shepherds speak.

The play turns its light form to dark purpose, as clowning and pastoral talk give way to tragedy repeating itself, like an aria returning to its opening. Readers and small theatre groups will find a compact, haunting work, easy to stage and hard to forget. It suits those who enjoy Millay's lyric voice turned dramatic, and plays that say much in little time.
9594-the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittie:
Volume six of Whittier's works gathers three prose groups: Old Portraits and Modern Sketches, Personal Sketches and Tributes, and Historical Papers. Old portraits range from John Bunyan and Andrew Marvell to Samuel Hopkins and Placido, the slave poet. Personal tributes honor Torrey, Everett, Channing, and Holmes. Historical papers take in Daniel O'Connell, the Pilgrims, and black men in the Revolution.

Taken whole, the volume shows Whittier as essayist and historian, not just poet. His sketches praise brave, plain folk and trace freedom's cause through lives. A reader gets a rich store of Whittier prose, full of moral portraiture and New England memory.
aria-da-capo:
Aria da Capo, a play in one act by Edna St Vincent Millay and copyrighted in 1920, stages a harlequinade that tragedy keeps interrupting. Millay sets a long banquet table in a black and white interior, with Pierrot in lilac and Columbine in pink dining at either end. Their talk is pure confection: macaroons, artichokes, and kisses promised for Tuesdays, though the day, Columbine corrects him, is Wednesday.

Then Cothurnus, the masque of tragedy, claims the stage and makes the shepherds Thyrsis and Corydon play out a scene of envy that ends in real killing, paper flowers and all. The lovers resume their banquet as if nothing had happened, and the play's title, meaning sing it again from the top, becomes an accusation. Millay wrote the piece as the Great War ended, and its pretty cycle of violence needs no date to bite.
britannica-1911-almodovar-del-campo:
Coal, more than its old fortress walls, explains modern Almodóvar del Campo. The Spanish town lies in Ciudad Real province, eighteen miles south-south-west of the capital, below the Sierra de Alcúdia's northern slopes. In 1900 it counted 12,525 people. Medieval Almodóvar was a Moorish stronghold, yet little there now draws students of old buildings.

Three miles south sits the rich Puertollano coal-field, linked by a branch line of the railway running from Madrid through Badajoz to Lisbon, and mining drives the town's growth. Local hands make lace and linen, while trade in live-stock, oil, and wine stays brisk. Beyond the sierra, the crown-owned Alcúdia valley serves as grazing land for huge sheep flocks.
britannica-1911-baldinucci-filippo:
Filippo Baldinucci (1624–1696) was an Italian writer on the history of art, born at Florence. His chief work bears the title Notizie de' Professori del Disegno da Cimabue and covers artists from 1260 to 1670. It came out in six volumes between 1681 and 1728.

The 1911 Britannica entry praises the scale of the work but flags its main flaw: Baldinucci tried to trace all Italian art back to the schools of Florence. A good edition by Ranalli, in five volumes at Florence in 1845–1847, is named for readers. His full works were printed at Milan in fourteen volumes in 1808–1812.
britannica-1911-brunelleschi-filippo:
Filippo Brunelleschi (1379–1446) was an Italian architect, the reviver in Italy of the Roman or Classic style, born at Florence in 1379. His father, a notary, had destined him for that profession, but seeing the boy's talent for all kinds of mechanism placed him in the goldsmiths' guild. He quickly became a skilled workman and perfected himself in sculpture, perspective and geometry.

In 1401 he competed for the design of the gates of the baptistery of San Giovanni and lost, though his work won praise, and soon afterward set out for Rome. Hard study there fixed his resolve to revive the older classical style, dead in Italy. He was among the first to apply the scientific laws of perspective to his work. Back in Florence in 1407, as the city resolved to complete Santa Maria del Fiore cathedral, his plan for a cupola was approved, though only in 1419.
britannica-1911-casanova-de-seingalt-gio:
Giovanni Jacopo Casanova de Seingalt (1725–1798) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian adventurer born at Venice. His father came from an old, even noble family but angered his friends by taking up acting. His mother, Zanetta Farusi, was the beautiful daughter of a Venetian shoemaker. His grandmother raised him and had him educated far above her means.

At sixteen Casanova entered the seminary of St Cyprian in Venice. He was soon expelled for scandalous conduct and escaped prison only through his mother's efforts, which placed him in the household of Cardinal Acquaviva. Restraint irked him, and he took to travel. Rome, Naples, Corfu, and Constantinople followed. He was by turns journalist, preacher, abbé, and diplomatist, but held no role long. The entry frames a life of adventure and intrigue that ran until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aleppo:
Aleppo is an Armenian Rite archdiocese in Syria, centred on a city standing on eight little hills in an oasis between the Orontes and the Euphrates. Arab tradition says Abraham lived there and gave milk to all comers, giving the town its name Haleb, while Seleucus Nicator renamed it Beroea. It passed from the Seljukids and other medieval rulers to the Ottoman Turks in 1317, apart from an Egyptian occupation from 1833 to 1839.

In ancient times Aleppo was a trading depot between India, the Tigris and Euphrates lands, and the Mediterranean. It still forwarded the goods of Diyarbekir, Mosul, and Baghdad to Alexandria. Its population of about 127,000 included some 19,200 Catholics of several rites, governed by four Catholic archbishops. Muslims, Jews, and other Christians lived alongside them. French Catholic missions centred there, with Carmelites from 1625, Lazarists, Jesuits from 1873, and Capuchin missions, and the city counted 260 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-augustine-:
St. Augustine of Hippo is known through documents of unrivalled richness, and this entry sketches his life in three periods. Of no great character of ancient times do we have information comparable to the Confessions, which tell the touching story of his soul. The Retractations give the history of his mind, and the Life by his friend Possidius tells of his apostolate. The three periods are the young wanderer's gradual return to the faith. They are the doctrinal growth of the Christian philosopher to his episcopate, and the full growth of his work on the episcopal throne of Hippo.

Augustine was born at Tagaste on 13 November 354. Tagaste, now Souk-Ahras, lay about sixty miles from Bona, the ancient Hippo-Regius. The entry follows the boy of Tagaste through sin and searching to baptism, then through the bishop's battles with heresy and his books, which shaped Western theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-poppo:
Poppo, abbot and monastic reformer, carried Cluniac renewal through Flanders and the empire. Born in 977 to the Flemish nobles Tizekinus and Adalwif, he made pilgrimages to the Holy Land and Rome. A flame bursting over his head on a night journey, with his lance shining, convinced him to seek another life, and in 1005 he entered St Thierry at Reims.

Abbot Richard of St Vannes took him to Verdun, made him prior of St Vaast at Arras about 1013, and then of Beaulieu. There he reclaimed monastic lands from rapacious vassals and secured them by deeds. Emperor Henry II later set him over Stavelot and other houses. He died at Marchiennes on 25 January 1048, a reformer of discipline and property alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teaching-of-s:
This entry treats the teaching and influence of St Augustine of Hippo, who lived from 354 to 430. Schaff calls him a genius of the first order, dominating antiquity and later ages like a pyramid. Among theologians he stands undeniably first, and no Father, Scholastic, or Reformer has surpassed his influence. His life and writings are treated elsewhere, and here his teaching falls into three parts: his function as Doctor of the Church, his system of grace, and Augustinism in history.

Augustine ruled a third-rate city and barely touched politics, lacking, as Harnack notes, a statesman's gifts. His place apart rests on thought, felt beyond theology. Critics now concede his intellectual influence unrivalled, even by Aquinas. The entry weighs his rank, the elements of his influence, the qualities of his doctrine, and the character of his genius, closing on free will and salvation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wipo:
Wipo was an eleventh-century Burgundian chaplain to Emperor Konrad II and the emperor's lively biographer. Apparently a native of Burgundy, he lived in the first half of the eleventh century. As Konrad's chaplain he wrote the Gesta Chuonradi II Imperatoris in chronicle form and presented it to Konrad's son Henry III in 1046, soon after Henry's crowning. Wipo grasps his subject with freshness and warmth, yet he is no mere flatterer, seeing Konrad's faults plainly.

What Wipo misses is the wider age: the emperor's tangled dealings with princes and Church escape his full grasp. His style stays simple, fluent, and well chosen. His surviving works include the Proverbia maxims of 1027 or 1028, and the Tetralogus Heinrici in rhymed hexameters for Henry in 1041, praising right and law as the throne's true base. The Easter sequence Victimae Paschali Laudes, and a moving Latin lament on Konrad's death, complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-works-of-st-a:
Works of Saint Augustine surveys the output of one of humanity's most prolific minds, praised for range. Augustine, bishop from 354 to 430, casts thought in powerful forms: Bardenhewer lauds his supple speech and gift for painting the soul's inward states. His Latin bears his age's stamp, noble and chaste, dropping in sermons to the people's tongue. No full analysis fits here, so the entry maps his chief writings with dates.

Autobiography and letters come first: Confessions, about 400, praise God at work in a soul rather than merely confessing sins, unmatched for soul analysis, feeling, and depth. Retractations, from 426 to 428, revises his works in order, explaining each occasion and idea, a priceless guide to his growth. His 270 letters, 53 from correspondents, treasure his life, sway, and teaching. Philosophy dialogues from Cassiciacum, City of God begun in 413 against pagans blaming Rome's fall on ended worship, and many more follow.
ceylon-an-account-of-the-island-physical:
Sir James Emerson Tennent's account of Ceylon reached a fourth, thoroughly revised edition at London in 1860, and this first volume treats the island's physical side. Contents run from geology and gems to rivers, coasts, and harbours. Ancient geographers' errors about the island's size are corrected, and Adam's Bridge and the mountain system get full treatment.

Natural history fills the later parts: eagles, parrots, pigeons, jungle-fowl, and flamingoes, then shells, starfish, beetles, and dragonflies. Local detail is dense — a harmless black millipede in Colombo gardens, another with a crimson band down its back. Maps, plans, and drawings support the text. Tennent wrote as a colonial official with years on the island.
dio-s-rome-volume-1-an-historical-narrat:
What is left of Dio's lost early books fills this first volume of his Rome, in English by Herbert Baldwin Foster. The Pafraets Book Company of Troy, New York, issued it in 1905. Foster, of Lehigh University, inscribes it to his teacher Gildersleeve of Baltimore.

Two gleanings make the book. First comes the epitome of books one to twenty-one by Ioannes Zonaras, a soldier and secretary who wrote in the monastery of Mount Athos about 1130. Fragments of books twenty-two to thirty-five follow. A sample tells how Carthage bought an armistice with money, grain, and hostages, yielding Sicily and the islands round it to Rome. The volume is a rescue job: a great history kept in scraps.
dio-s-rome-volume-2-an-historical-narrat:
Books thirty-six to forty-four of Dio's Roman history fill this second volume, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905. The Pafraets Book Company of Troy, New York, issued it. The span in years is 69 to 44 before Christ, the fall of the republic.

Book thirty-six opens with Metellus forcing Crete, and Mithridates and Tigranes renewing their war. Lucullus takes Tigranocerta and Nisibis, then loses ground as his army rises against him. Pirates grow insolent and draw a war of their own. Caesar fills the later books: amnesty for beaten foes, then garrisons, fines, and tribute to humble the rest. The style is spare annals, year by year, in Foster's close rendering.
dio-s-rome-volume-3-an-historical-narrat:
Books forty-five to fifty-one of Dio's history fill this third volume, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1906. The span is 44 to 29 before Christ, from Caesar's murder to the new order. Contents name each book at the head, with summaries in the old manner.

Book forty-five treats Gaius Octavius, afterward named Augustus, and Sextus, the son of Pompey. Caesar and Antony fall into open strife, and Cicero speaks his great harangue against Antony. In Africa, Sextius holds Numidia against stronger foes sent for Caesar's side, and grows proud as they delay. Triumvirs, proscriptions, and sea war fill the set. The volume is Dio on the republic's death throes, in plain English dress.
dio-s-rome-volume-4-an-historical-narrat:
Books fifty-two to sixty of Dio's history fill this fourth volume, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905. The Pafraets Book Company of Troy, New York, issued it. The span runs from 29 before Christ to the year 54 after, the first emperors.

Book fifty-two opens with Caesar weighing whether to lay down his power. Dio marks the turn: seven hundred and twenty-five years of kings, democracy, and the rule of a few, then monarchy again. Augustus, Tiberius, and their house fill the books that follow. A march through German woods, in tight ranks against attacks, shows the wars on the edge of the empire. The volume joins set speeches to hard campaigning.
dio-s-rome-volume-5-an-historical-narrat:
Books sixty-one onward of Dio's history fill this fifth volume, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1906. The span runs from the year 54 to 211 after Christ. Nero seizes the sovereignty in the first summary, and the tone is set at once.

Young Nero yields at first to his mother, till Seneca and Burrus push her from control. Wanton shows, the death of Silanus, love for Acte, and the slaying of Britannicus follow in Dio's list. Seneca's own faults get a section of blame. Later books cross rivers against barbarians who break at the sight of a fleet from a treeless land. Emperors rise and fall in Dio's dry order, each weighed as he passes.
dio-s-rome-volume-6-an-historical-narrat:
The last books of Dio's history fill this sixth volume, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905. The Pafraets Book Company of Troy, New York, issued it. Books seventy-seven to eighty cover the years 211 to 229 after Christ, and fragments, a glossary, and a general index close the set.

Book seventy-seven opens with Antoninus, called Caracalla, killing his brother Geta and many more. Papinian and Cilo suffer his cruelty, and he plays at being a second Alexander. Levies, waste, treachery to kings, and massacres at Alexandria fill his reign in Dio's telling. The fragments then run back to Rome's first books, with Cloelia given arms and a horse by Porsenna. The volume ends the six-part English Dio.
doe-osti-17047516-development-of-the-reh:
Gustavo Campos, Sertac Akar, and Parthiv Kurup of the National Laboratory of the Rockies built a proof of concept tool called ReHeat, described in September 2026. ReHeat helps planners judge hybrid industrial process heat systems, which mix several heating technologies to supply factory heat. Choosing among boilers, solar collectors, heat pumps, and storage is a cost puzzle with many moving parts.

An optimization model weighs life cycle cost, capital and running costs, heat balance, and available land area. A district heating case study runs the tool through base case winter and summer operation. Sensitivity charts then vary thermal storage cost and solar collector cost to show how the best system mix shifts with prices.
doe-osti-2588681-site-a-and-plot-m-2024-:
Collin Klimek and Jordan Vopat of Argonne National Laboratory prepared this surveillance and inspection report, ANL-25/01, dated September 2025. Site A and Plot M are Manhattan Project-era burial grounds in the forest preserves southwest of Chicago, holding waste from the earliest reactor work. Argonne still watches them, decades after closure.

The report pairs 2024 environmental surveillance with the 2025 annual inspection. Monitoring tracks hydrogen-3 in the streams next to Plot M, in Site A area ponds, and in monitoring wells. Strontium-90 gets its own well measurements. Six wells cased into the dolomite bedrock, downgradient of Plot M in Red Gate Woods, were sampled in 2024 to follow hydrogen-3 moving through the aquifer. Inspection results are reported for Red Gate Woods, Plot M, and Site A in turn, with issues, improvement opportunities, and corrective actions listed.
doe-osti-2589491-thermal-management-for-:
Cooperative project CRD-17-00683 with John Deere Electronic Solutions closes with National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5700-96477. Technical contact Emily Cousineau covers computer modeling of heat flow in flat semiconductor packages. The parts use silicon carbide devices inside an inverter for off-road vehicles, where cooling space is tight and heat can kill electronics.

The partners built two- and three-dimensional design models of the package and tested cooling layouts in simulation. Options included cooling from both faces of the flat package, air cooling, and liquid cooling. The partner supplied operating conditions and design limits drawn from industry needs. The goal was the most effective cooling at the lowest added product cost. Results guide packaging choices for rugged vehicle power electronics.
doe-osti-3000943-hanford-site-raptor-nes:
J. J. Nugent and Cole Lindsey of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions report two breeding seasons of nest monitoring across the Hanford Site in Washington, dated September 2025. The old nuclear reservation's shrub-steppe hosts nesting raptors and ravens, and cleanup work must steer around them. Surveyors mapped raptor and common raven nests over the portion of the site managed by Hanford Field Operations in 2024 and 2025.

One species gets special attention. Seventeen traditional ferruginous hawk nesting territories were tracked, with occupancy checks in late May and productivity counts in June each year. Ferruginous hawks are large, ground-and-platform nesting birds sensitive to disturbance, and the Hanford population is watched closely. Results tables and nest maps record which territories were occupied and how the pairs fared, feeding the site's wildlife compliance planning. The report is the routine annual account for calendar years 2024 and 2025.
doe-osti-3001260-hybrid-quantum-networks:
Shengwang Du of the University of Texas at Dallas leads a five-university team in the final report for award DE-SC0022069. It covers September 2021 to August 2025, on joining two rival dialects of quantum information. Discrete-variable systems encode qubits in single photon properties like polarisation: clean, low-error, but fiddly. Continuous-variable systems encode in the smooth quadratures of light fields: deterministic and efficient, but differently flawed. A quantum internet needs both kinds of node talking.

The team created hybrid entanglement, linking a single photon's polarisation to the quadrature variables of an optical cat state, a superposition of two light pulses. Around that resource they built toward a hybrid quantum local area network over fibre. Entanglement generation, swapping and distribution between unlike nodes were the aims. A wavelength converter carrying polarisation qubits from near-infrared to telecom bands was also developed. Results and publications fill the report.
doe-osti-3001625-roughrider-carbon-stora:
Wesley Peck, Kyle Glazewski, Carrie Christianson and colleagues at the University of North Dakota deliver the Roughrider Carbon Storage Hub final report. It is 2025-EERC-11-01, dated November 2025, for cooperative agreement DE-FE0032282. The work ran October 2023 to September 2025 near North Dakota's oil country. It tested whether the Inyan Kara and Broom Creek formations could store carbon dioxide at hub scale.

A dedicated characterisation well, Roughrider 1, anchored the study with core analysis and testing, joined by seismic interpretation of existing data. Geologic models fed dynamic simulations across scenario tables. Single injection wells sat at depths near 5,600 and 7,800 feet. Bottomhole pressure limits ran between 2,100 and 3,000 psi, and temperatures around 172 to 207 degrees Fahrenheit. Key findings chapters translate the simulations into storage implications. The report closes two years of site science for a proposed Williston Basin storage hub.
doe-osti-3002154-technical-background-an:
Jesse G. Smith Jr., Christian Mark G. Salvador, Fredrick G. Dolislager, and eight colleagues document a health-risk tool in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4166, dated September 2025. The tool is the Residential Water Inhalation Risk Calculator, hosted on the Risk Assessment Information System. It estimates what people breathe in from chemicals that escape tap water during showers and other household use.

Unlike older models that use one fixed constant, this calculator tracks gas levels over time in three linked spaces: shower, bathroom, and living room. The report explains the math, defines the shower scenario and its variables, and gives page-by-page user guides. It also compares results with the ATSDR calculator, including runs with bathroom doors open or closed and exhaust fans on or off.
doe-osti-3005992-degradable-biocomposite:
Final technical report DE-EE0009296 from UC San Diego, led by Jonathan Pokorski, covers degradable biocomposite thermoplastic polyurethanes, or TPUs, made with bacterial spores as filler. The team screened bacteria and picked Bacillus subtilis ATCC 6633 for its sporulation and TPU-eating activity. Adaptive lab evolution then bred a heat-shock tolerant strain whose germination after heat shock ran 17.7 times the wild type.

Dry spore powder went in during hot melt extrusion at 135 degrees C. The tolerant strain kept near 100 percent viability through extrusion, against about 20 percent for the wild type, and the spores stiffened the plastic: toughness rose up to 37 percent. In autoclaved compost the tolerant-strain composite lost 92 percent of its mass in five months, versus 44 percent for plain TPU. Respirometry showed 72 percent biomineralized to carbon dioxide in six months. Pilot extrusion at 30 times lab throughput and injection molding both retained the gains.
doe-osti-3014287-an-assessment-of-techni:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/3940, led by Carly Hansen and Juan Gallego-Calderon with eight co-authors from Oak Ridge and Idaho National Laboratory, assesses hydropower potential at America's non-powered dams. Only about 3 percent of nationally inventoried dams generate electricity. The rest were built for water supply, navigation, flood control, or recreation, and many could host turbines without new dam construction.

The assessment covers more than 2,600 non-powered dams with a collective potential of nearly 4 gigawatts of new capacity. Methods estimate generation and capacity factor from flow records and hydraulic head, with monthly head patterns derived from dam dimensions and primary purpose. The report updates earlier national assessments with better data, giving developers a screened list of the most promising existing dams.
doe-osti-3015559-landcast-mosaic-reconst:
Fifty years of world population maps are reconstructed in LandCast Mosaic, an Oak Ridge technical report dated November 2025 by Zimmer, Adams, and Urban. Planners need population grids for years between censuses, so the team rebuilt global distributions from 1975 to 2025 by fusing modern data backward in time.

The method starts from the LandScan Mosaic 2025 grid and the Global Human Settlement Layer's built-surface record. Because the two rasters share a nominal three arc-second resolution but sit on offset grids, each LandScan pixel overlaps four settlement pixels, which are aggregated to match. Interpolation then carries built surface and population through the decades. The result is a consistent half-century population surface for exposure, planning, and risk work.
doe-osti-3020423-pv-lifetime-project-202:
National Laboratory of the Rockies annual report NLR/TP-5K00-98639, by Chris Deline and six co-authors, gives the 2025 snapshot of the PV Lifetime Project. DOE started the project in 2016 to buy commercial solar modules, deploy them outdoors, and measure precisely how their performance fades. The laboratory and Sandia have fielded more than 950 samples from 12 manufacturers across sites in New Mexico, Colorado, and Florida.

Modules from makers such as Jinko, Trina, Canadian Solar, Hanwha, LG, and Panasonic sit in long-term field arrays, with output checked year after year. The report compiles the fleet and its measured performance at the laboratory's site. Long records like these let buyers, insurers, and manufacturers separate genuinely durable designs from weak ones, and they anchor the degradation rates used in solar project finance.
doe-osti-3020499-fy2016-ilaw-glass-spft-:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-17R3860-1, by Adonia E. Papathanassiu, Charles Viragh, Isabelle S. Muller, and Ian L. Pegg, presents fiscal year 2016 dissolution testing of immobilized low-activity waste glass. Published in July 2017 and released under HFO-73168, the work supports Hanford's Integrated Disposal Facility, where this glass will be buried on site. Regulators need to know how fast the glass breaks down in water over long times.

The team ran single-pass flow-through tests, which flow water past glass at fixed rates, on glass composition IDF7-E12. Test matrices covered 23, 40, 70, and 90 degrees Celsius at several pH values. Boron release served as the tracer for overall glass dissolution. The measured rates feed the facility's performance assessment, the long-range safety case for the disposal site.
doe-osti-3022414-advanced-test-reactor-l:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-88472, by Dani Ottaway and Kelly McCary, reports coolant loop activity at the Advanced Test Reactor for cycle 175B-1, which ran from August 4 to October 6, 2025. Gamma-ray spectrometry of loop liquid samples measures which radionuclides circulate in the coolant and how well the purification system removes them.

Results are tabulated sample by sample for each loop, with radionuclide concentrations, measurement uncertainties, and decontamination factors computed as the ratio between ion exchanger inlet and outlet samples. The data pages record sampling dates and times alongside values for nuclides such as argon-41 and manganese-54, giving reactor chemists a cycle-specific picture of coolant quality and cleanup performance. It is a routine surveillance record in the laboratory's long-running series for this reactor.
doe-osti-3023581-wec-irradiation-can-the:
Ryan Patrick Wilkerson and Erik Paul Luther of Los Alamos National Laboratory report thermal testing of irradiation cans for Westinghouse Electric, in LA-UR-26-22107, issued March 18, 2026. A long list of contributors joins them. The cans hold material during irradiation, and the tests check how hydrogen behaves inside them at temperature. Specimens were run at temperatures up to 900 degrees.

Hydrogen-to-metal ratios were measured three ways: in-can, out-of-can, and by LECO analysis with mass correction. The SWIFT model matched the in-can measurements. Alumina coatings applied by atomic layer deposition, at 100 and 200 nanometers, showed no clear effect on hydrogen loss. Rankings of coated and native specimens flipped between measurement methods, so the authors conclude a significant effect on internal hydrogen retention is unlikely.
doe-osti-3377123-lamp-technical-readines:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LAMP-ENG-RPT-003, Revision 2, issued July 7, 2026 as LA-UR-26-25566, grades the readiness of the LAMP accelerator project's parts. R. W. Garnett and J. W. Lewellen wrote it for the National Nuclear Security Administration's Office of Experimental Science, NA-113. LAMP is the planned upgrade path for the LANSCE linac. It asks which parts are proven hardware and which are still paper. Each item gets a technology readiness level.

Choppers slice the beam into pulses early in the line. The team weighs the 3-MeV medium energy beam transport chopper against units at CERN's Linac 4, at RAL-ISIS, and at Oak Ridge's Spallation Neutron Source. Tables score beam energy, deflector length, voltage, and rise time against set marks. The LAMP chopper pulser system rates TRL 5. CERN's unit meets the energy and timing marks but not the voltage mark. The verdicts steer which designs to copy or rework.
doe-osti-3413709-nsuf-yhx-irradiation-te:
Oak Ridge status report ORNL/LTR-2026/4729, dated August 2026, tracks irradiation testing of yttrium hydride samples in the High Flux Isotope Reactor. A. G. Le Coq, K. M. Krogh, M. N. Cinbiz, and K. D. Linton wrote the update. The work sits under the NSUF user program.

Six capsules completed irradiation after reactor cycle 514 ended in March 2026. Two facility types were used: one for partial cycles, one for full cycles. Tables give each capsule's heat, duration, position, and fast fluence. Yttrium hydride is a candidate moderator for compact reactors, so checked test records guide later exams.
doe-osti-3580364-all-polyester-multilaye:
Michigan State University's final technical report, submitted in March 2026, closes a project led by Muhammad Rabnawaz. Partners were Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Amcor Global. The project ran from June 2022 to the end of 2025 under a cooperative agreement. Its aim was to redesign multilayer plastic packaging, which is hard to recycle because its layers use unlike materials.

The team built six test films made only from polyester, using standard cast-film and co-extrusion methods. Tests checked barrier strength, toughness, and sealing. Both mechanical and chemical recycling paths were shown to work. Cost studies found the most advanced films at cost parity, or about twelve percent below current commercial films. Life-cycle work also pointed to lower energy use and lower greenhouse gas output.
doe-osti-3683716-near-repository-investi:
Sandia report SAND2026-25691R, dated September 30, 2025, models the ground near a planned repository for hot spent nuclear fuel. Seven authors are printed, led by Eduardo Basurto, Tara LaForce, and Laura P. Swiler. The host rock is argillite, a fine clay-rich rock. Hot waste packages heat the rock around them, so near-field behaviour drives the safety case. The work sits in the Spent Fuel and Waste Science and Technology Campaign.

A refined model covers one quarter of a waste package and its shale setting. Layers include the package, a two-clay buffer, the disturbed rock zone, and host shale. Depth and heat output values are drawn from past studies, with a table of decay heat by package type. The Geologic Disposal Safety Assessment framework drives the runs. Its tools pair PFLOTRAN flow modelling with Dakota for sampling and uncertainty checks. Workflow files are printed in appendices for reruns.
doe-osti-3685161-site-a-and-plot-m-2025-:
Argonne report ANL-26/01, dated September 2026, pairs the 2025 surveillance results and the 2026 inspection for Site A and Plot M. Collin Klimek of Argonne's Environment, Safety, and Health Directorate prepared it for the Office of Legacy Management. Site A and Plot M are old reactor and burial grounds near the lab, now in long-term care. Many lab staff fed data and figures into the volume.

Monitoring covers streams and ponds by Plot M, groundwater under both sites, and the Red Gate Woods area. Tables report hydrogen-3 and strontium-90 levels in stream, pond, and well water on set 2025 dates. Some wells are slant wells drilled at an angle to forty feet. Inspection chapters then walk each area in turn, with photographs of current conditions. Issues, chances to improve, and corrective actions close the report.
doe-osti-3799246-thermodynamics-of-triti:
A Pacific Northwest study dated September 2026 asks whether crystal defects in coating layers can catch and hold tritium. Michel Sassi, David Senor, and Andrew Casella are the printed authors. Tritium bred in reactor pellets slowly leaks through cladding into coolant water. An aluminum coating on the steel slows that leak. Where coating meets steel, chromium-rich phases form, and empty atom sites inside them might trap stray tritium.

Computer models tested four such phases, from a chromium silicide to chromium-aluminum mixes. In each, empty metal sites pulled tritium in with strength to spare. Silicon vacancies in the silicide phase trapped hardest. Trapped tritium always bonded to chromium, never to silicon or aluminum. Heat and gas pressure shifts were folded into the sums. The ranking matches earlier work on iron-aluminum phases.
doe-osti-3895827-2025-aser-annual-site-e:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28407, issued September 18, 2026, is the laboratory's Annual Site Environmental Report for 2025. Eight authors are printed, led by Renee Robinson, Nell Larson, and Shannon Gaukler. Federal rules require the lab to report its environmental footprint each year. Chapters track air emissions, radiation, water quality, weather, and cleanup progress.

The site's water story runs in three layers: shallow canyon alluvium, perched pockets in the tuff, and the regional aquifer below. The report lets regulators and neighbours check the lab's claims against raw results. Quality assurance sections explain sample handling and data management. Long-term climate trends put the year's weather in perspective. The lab frames the work as stewardship: cut risk through legacy cleanup and prevent pollution. A magazine-style summary is published alongside the full volume.
doe-osti-3935723-characterizing-the-elec:
Fermilab hosted a summer 2026 faculty project on the slow extraction of particle beams, reported here as FERMILAB-FN-1301-CSAID. James Dolen of Purdue University Northwest led the work, with Nhan Tran of Fermilab as co-lead and students Matthew Prescott and Thomas Osborn. The hosted text covers beam spills, not the detector topic in the catalog title.

High-power experiments need beam drawn off in a smooth stream, since spikes can swamp detectors. The team shifted focus from Main Injector extraction for SpinQuest to Delivery Ring extraction for the Mu2e experiment. They built a data pipeline that lines up instrument channels and picks out clean spills. Tests with a quadrupole pulse mapped how the beam responds over time. The results feed digital twin models and neural network controllers that steady the Mu2e spill in real time.
folk-tales-of-napoleon-napoleonder-from-:
Amfiteatrov and Balzac meet in Folk-Tales of Napoleon, translated by George Kennan in 1902. Aleksandr Amfiteatrov gives Napoleonder, the tale as Russian peasants told it. Their name for Napoleon, Kennan notes, adds a syllable, as if the word were clipped without it. In the tale, God calls a council of angels to punish a wicked world.

Honoré de Balzac's Napoleon of the People makes the second half. An old soldier tells the tale in his own voice. He marched to Toulon on the way to Egypt, while the English sent their warships to catch the fleet. Napoleon told the men the English would never see them, for his star would guide them. They took Malta, he says, as one picks an orange in passing. The book shows Napoleon remade by the folk who fought him and the folk who followed him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PittsburghPostG:
Bob Hoover, the book editor of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, wrote this essay for the paper's Arts and Entertainment section. His subject is the rise of conspiracy thinking in American life. He opens with three investigated deaths: the playwright Christopher Marlowe, Lee Oswald, and Vincent Foster.

That opening trio does the essay's work. Suspicion, Hoover shows, is not new and not confined to one party or century. Marlowe's death was argued over in the 1590s; Foster's suicide in the 1990s drew the same machinery of doubt. The essay treats conspiracy as a habit of mind with a long history. It gives readers a newspaper editor's survey of why such stories spread and why they last.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SarentiLipo_Sar: From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers. An obscure item, complete, filed. A bare file, kept as issued. Subject: government records. nsia-SarentiLipo Sarenti Lipo: the made public government document, captured as titled.
govdocs-archive_org-the-wisdom-of-ancien: The Wisdom of Ancient Cosmology: Contemporary Science in Light of Tradition - the made public government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated entry, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
nasa-tm-19630010644-design-analysis-of-a:
Six Lewis Research Center engineers wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-28. R. H. Cavicchi and H. H. Ellerbrock lead the author list. Their subject is a nuclear-powered cargo plane that flies below sound speed. Its reactor is cooled by helium gas, not water or air.

A nuclear plane could fly for weeks without refueling. That range suited heavy logistics work for the air force. The team worked out the design on paper, reactor and all. They weighed thrust, weight, shielding, and safety for the layout. The study dates to the bold years when atomic flight seemed near, and it shows the hard trade-offs that grounded the idea.
nasa-tm-19670005891-the-feasibility-of-a:
P. E. Schmid, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this study on September 1, 1966. It asks whether communication satellites of the 1970s could relay Apollo spacecraft data directly to a fixed station on Earth. Ground stations lost contact whenever a spacecraft passed beyond their horizon, leaving gaps in coverage.

Schmid considered relay satellites in 24-hour synchronous orbits and in lower 6-hour orbits. The relay would carry Unified S-Band ranging, telemetry, voice, and Doppler data, plus Apollo's VHF voice signal. The study found the main constraint was antenna pointing between the satellite and the Apollo capsule. Using omnidirectional antennas on both ends removed the pointing problem, though at a cost in signal strength. Feasibility, Schmid concludes, turns on how much antenna complexity is allowed.
nasa-tm-19670009725-tropospheric-and-ion:
E. Hirschmann, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in January 1967. It examines how two layers of air, the troposphere and the ionosphere, disturb radio communication. The work supported LOCAST, a project to locate aircraft by satellite transponder.

The paper's main purpose is a realistic estimate of the atmosphere's influence. Hirschmann focuses on errors in range and range-rate measurements. Those errors decide which operating frequency a system should choose. With the right frequency, a satellite at synchronous altitude could fix the position of a high-speed aircraft precisely. The introduction explains how signal deterioration arises in each layer.
nasa-tm-19670074061-postlaunch-report-fo:
Mission AS-201 gets its official reckoning in this postlaunch report, issued May 6, 1966, by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas. AS-201 flew Apollo Spacecraft 009. Postlaunch reports are the program's own record of what a mission did.

The front matter includes a table called Apollo Spacecraft Flight History. It lists the program's earlier tests in order. Pad abort and transonic abort tests at White Sands appear first, from late 1963. Nominal launch tests from Cape Kennedy follow through 1964. The table frames AS-201 as the next step in that test ladder. It stands as the flight's formal closing record, kept for later crews and engineers.
nasa-tm-19680027694-pulsational-instabil:
Norman R. Simon and Richard Stothers of the Institute for Space Studies at Goddard Space Flight Center study pulsating stars in this paper, part one of a series. Their subjects are massive blue stars with helium cores and thin, hydrogen-poor envelopes. Such stars can swell and shrink in regular pulsations, or stay stable.

Core structure barely changed when the hydrogen envelope was modified, they found. Total radius and luminosity did respond to envelope hydrogen content and gradient. Models stayed stable under modest central condensation conditions. Unstable models drew nearly all their energy from helium reactions in the core. Most damping happened in the thin non-burning hydrogen envelope. Pulsation periods stayed remarkably steady for each mass.
nasa-tm-19690011506-performance-of-an-ex:
Robert P. Macosko, William T. Hanna, Sol H. Gorland, and Kent S. Jefferies of Lewis Research Center report a long SNAP-8 power system test in this report. The experimental system ran for well over a thousand hours at Lewis. About eleven hundred hours of that running was continuous operation.

Steady-state performance did not degrade with time, the authors found. All prototype components performed satisfactorily except the parasitic load resistor, which failed during testing. Three automatic shutdowns occurred, and the protective system functioned properly each time. One erratic start flooded the mercury boiler with pressure and flow excursions. Even so, steady operation afterward was unaffected, and no oil contaminated the mercury loop.
nasa-tm-19710015102-the-potential-of-nuc:
G R Seikel and L D Nichols of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 propulsion meeting in Salt Lake City. It weighs nuclear MHD power systems for space and ground use. An MHD generator passes hot ionized gas through a magnetic field to make electricity directly. Very hot reactors make the idea attractive.

The study compared three power cycles built around such generators. A turbine assisted MHD cycle came out most attractive. It offered high efficiency with a modest radiator for space use. The authors also sized a large shielded space system. A ground station reaching about sixty percent efficiency also looked possible.
nasa-tm-19710028093-computer-program-for:
Lona M Howser and Stephen S Tompkins of the Langley Research Center documented a computer program for ablating bodies. An ablating body sheds its surface layer by layer under fierce heating, as a reentry heat shield does. Their program follows the time changing response of round symmetric bodies. It also tracks how the shape itself changes as material burns away. Earlier tools often froze the shape in place.

The report presents the program in full detail. Every subroutine and variable is listed and defined. Three worked sample problems show the printed and plotted output. That material helps a new user set up and run a case. The governing equation and solution method are also explained.
podcast-dannyjones-o5zBnkfDWpo:
Journalist Thomas Morton joins Danny Jones to tell tales from his years at VICE. The episode title names his trips into Scientology and North Korea, and rot in the media. Morton was one of the faces of VICE TV.

Morton tells how he got inside closed lands and groups with a camera and a grin. He shares what North Korea felt like from the ground and what Scientology showed him. Jones asks what broke at VICE as it grew. Listeners get wild field tales from a gonzo pro. The library keeps the talk as an archive record of his years on the road.
selections-from-american-poetry-with-spe:
Margaret Sprague Carhart edited this gathering of American verse, with special weight on Poe, Longfellow, Lowell, and Whittier. Contents begin with Anne Bradstreet's Contemplation and Michael Wigglesworth's Day of Doom. Colonial and early national voices lead the way.

Phillip Freneau, Francis Hopkinson, and Samuel Woodworth follow, with songs like Hail Columbia and The Old Oaken Bucket. Later pages center on the four named poets of the title. Teachers and students get a compact tour of American poetry from Puritan times onward, mixing famed pieces with lesser-known work from the young nation's first singers.
the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittier-vol: Volume six of Whittier's works is shown by its contents list, with no essays following in this record. Old Portraits and Modern Sketches profiles John Bunyan and Richard Baxter. Personal sketches pay tribute to Longfellow and Lydia Maria Child. Historical papers cover Daniel O'Connell and the Pilgrims of Plymouth. The Black Men in the Revolution and War of 1812 is also listed. The pieces themselves do not appear in the pages present.
